newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Defence lawyer quits Port Arthur massacre case.
newsitem.headline: Defence lawyer quits Port Arthur massacre case.

text.p: The lawyer hired to defend the man accused of Australia's worst mass killing in modern times has resigned from the case, just days after Martin Bryant pleaded not guilty to all 35 murder charges.
"Media reports that I no longer represent Martin Bryant are correct," David Gunson said in a statement issued on Wednesday, two days after Bryant, 29, made his first appearance in court.
"I will make no further comment as to the reasons or circumstances surrounding this development," Gunson added.
Bryant is accused of opening fire at a popular tourist spot in the southern island state of Tasmania on April 28.

He wore a faint smile in Tasmania's Supreme Court here on Monday as he stood flanked by heavy security and denied all charges during a brief hearing attended by relatives of the murder victims and some survivors of the shooting.

Another Tasmania lawyer, John Avery, said later that he was likely to replace Gunson as Bryant's representative, but he needed to meet Bryant in his maximum-security prison cell on Thursday before deciding to take up the case.
"I think I'm likely to take it, but I have to sort it out with him tomorrow," Avery told Reuters in the Tasmanian capital, Hobart, on Wednesday afternoon.
Asked if the trial, tentatively set to begin on November 19, could be delayed due to the late change of defence counsel, Avery said: "At the end of the day, it's another murder case."
A basis for Bryant's not guilty pleas has neither been sought nor given so far, but the Supreme Court will discuss pre-trial issues at a hearing on Friday.
Bryant will not appear in court on Friday. He is being held in isolation in the hospital wing of Hobart's Risdon Prison and is banned contact with other inmates.
Among the total of 72 charges laid against Bryant are counts of attempted murder, wounding and arson.

Avery declined to comment on the prospects of finding an impartial jury to try the case, which has drawn blanket media coverage since the first shots were fired among the ruins of an old penal colony at Port Arthur on the island's southeast coast.
"That's something to look at down the track," he said.
But he added that the Supreme Court could select jurors from other Australian states if an impartial jury could not be found from within the island's population of around 500,000 people.
Avery declined any comment on Gunson's reason for quitting the case.
